Wide receiver Mike Evans will miss his third consecutive game, but Deebo Samuel is expected to return for the 49ers on Sunday.

The 49ers fully cleared Samuel to return for the team’s Week 10 game against the Dallas Cowboys. He has not played since Oct. 11, when he sustained a hamstring injury in a Week 5 win over the Seattle Seahawks.

The 49ers should get a further boost at wide receiver with the addition of veteran Keenan Allen, who will make his San Francisco debut after arriving in a midweek trade from the Indianapolis Colts.

“He’ll have a role,” 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said of Allen.

The 49ers acquired Allen at a time when the team has experienced an abundance of injuries at wide receiver. That list includes Evans, who left the Oct. 19 game against Washington due to Achilles tendinitis.

“It’s been going well,” Shanahan said. “I’m sure if this was the last game or something, he’d be able to go out there. But we’re just trying to make sure it fully heals so it doesn’t act up again. But it’s going in the right direction.”

text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- The Chiefs listed running back Kenneth Walker III as questionable for Sunday's road game against the Atlanta Falcons after he missed Friday's practice with a groin injury.

Coach Andy Reid said Walker reported tightness in his groin to the team in the morning before the Chiefs' final on-field practice of the week, resulting in the running back being held out of the session as a precautionary measure.

"We'll just see how he feels through this afternoon, with rehab and through tomorrow," Reid said. "Somewhere he tweaked it. We're kind of feeling it out just to see where we're at with that [groin]. We're not going to put him at risk. If he can go, he can go. If he can't, he can't."

Walker, who joined the Chiefs in March after signing a three-year, $43.05 million contract, has been one of the NFL's best offseason acquisitions. He enters Week 10 with 872 rushing yards, second in the league behind Atlanta's Bijan Robinson (880).

If Walker is unable to play, the Chiefs are expected to rely heavily on rookie running back Emmett Johnson, the fifth-round pick who has played most often on third downs. In eight games, Johnson has been effective as a runner (111 rushing yards and one touchdown on 26 attempts) and a receiver (237 yards and one touchdown on 14 receptions).

"He'll be ready to go," right guard Trey Smith said Friday regarding Johnson, who could make his first career start. "I like Emmett, man, his juice, his energy. He oozes enthusiasm, emotion and positive energy. You can tell the guy wants to be great, and you can tell he works at it. He really cares, man. I'm really excited for him. It's not hard to root for guys like that."

Meanwhile, the Chiefs expect to have wide receiver Xavier Worthy available after he left in the second half of last week's win over the Jets with a hamstring injury. That should take a little pressure off Josh Downs, who intends to play after being acquired from the Colts just before the NFL trade deadline Tuesday in an attempt to build out Kansas City's depth at the position.

"I thought he did a nice job for what we asked him to do, to digest everything in a couple days," Reid said of Downs. "He's a smart kid and knows how to play. He's been playing, which is great, and playing at a high level. He worked into the things we asked him to do and did well. I think he's ready to play in a game for us."

Downs had 33 catches for 354 yards and a touchdown in nine games with Indianapolis.

The Chiefs expect to have first-round pick Mansoor Delane back after the cornerback missed a couple of games with a shoulder injury. However, they likely will be without right tackle Jaylon Moore because of an ankle injury and Peter Woods due to a neck injury.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

A.J. Brown (ankle/knee) could return this week after a multi-week absence when the New England Patriots face the Detroit Lions in Munich. Brown traveled with the team to Germany and, along with running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee), has looked "pretty good" in practice this week, according to head coach Mike Vrabel.

Brown has been limited to three games this season and has been out since Week 7. He is listed as questionable for Sunday, along with Stevenson.

After sitting out last week while in concussion protocol, Deshaun Watson will be back under center for the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. Shedeur Sanders got the start against the New Orleans Saints in Week 9, but head coach Todd Monken announced this week that Watson is healthy enough to start.

Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III did not take part in Friday's practice after reporting a tight groin. Head coach Andy Reid said the NFL's second-leading rusher will get treatment and the team will see how he feels on Saturday before making a decision on his availability.

"We're feeling it out just to see. We're not going to put him at risk," said Reid. "If he can go, he'll go. If he can't, he can't."

Dallas Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens (hamstring) sounds ready to return after missing last week's win over the Indianapolis Colts. When asked if he'd be available Pickens told reporters, "When you turn that TV on, get some food, make sure if you have a wife or girlfriend, make sure you hug her, love her and when you turn the TV on you should see me."

Sam Darnold (ribs/quad) is expected to miss another week for the Seattle Seahawks with Drew Lock (right elbow/oblique) taking charge against the Las Vegas Raiders this week. Darnold missed a Week 9 win after suffering the injuries the week before against the Chicago Bears.

Willis has been playing through a groin injury and, after undergoing an MRI, it showed he is dealing with a core muscle issue. Nacua sustained his injuries in Week 9. description:
Nov 13 (Reuters) – Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson will miss between 6 to 10 weeks as he recovers from a broken and dislocated thumb, head coach Jesse Minter said on Friday.
Jackson, a two-time NFL Most Valuable Player, suffered the injury on the Ravens’ first offensive play in a November 1 game against the Buffalo Bills.
He could still return this season if the struggling Ravens can get back into the postseason picture.
His return was short-lived as he appeared to strike his throwing hand against the helmet of a Bills player before immediately leaving the field.
The Ravens, who have lost four consecutive games and are last in the AFC North division with a 4-5 record, host the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday.

Nov 13 (Reuters) – Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson will miss between 6 to 10 weeks as he recovers from a broken and dislocated thumb, head coach Jesse Minter said on Friday.

Jackson, a two-time NFL Most Valuable Player, suffered the injury on the Ravens’ first offensive play in a November 1 game against the Buffalo Bills. He could still return this season if the struggling Ravens can get back into the postseason picture.

“Recovery timelines are challenging to predict, but injuries like this that require surgery typically take about 6-10 weeks to heal,” Minter said in a statement. “He is doing everything he can to get back, and we will let his progress guide the timing of his return.”

Jackson made a strong start to the 2026 NFL season before missing three games with an ankle sprain suffered in a Week 4 clash against the Tennessee Titans.

His return was short-lived as he appeared to strike his throwing hand against the helmet of a Bills player before immediately leaving the field.

The Ravens, who have lost four consecutive games and are last in the AFC North division with a 4-5 record, host the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday.

text:
Heading into Week 10, New England ruled out starting CB Carlton Davis III (knee), C/G Ben Brown (knee), and RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness). The Patriots are also listing nine players as questionable for Sunday's game vs. the Lions: WR A.J. Brown (ankle/knee), RB Rhamondre Stevenson (knee), S Kevin Byard III (chest), TE Cameron Latu (back), OL Walter Rouse (concussion), S Brenden Schooler (hamstring), CB Charles Woods (hamstring), FB Reggie Gilliam (knee), and C/G Greg Van Roten (hamstring).

On offense, star wideout A.J. Brown returned to practice this week after sitting out the last two games with a knee injury that flared up in practice. Brown practiced in a limited capacity throughout the week and seems to be tracking toward returning as soon as Sunday. The Pats top wideout has played in only 3-of-9 games this season, catching nine passes for 101 receiving yards. Obviously, that's not the result anyone hoped for when the Patriots traded a 2028 first-round pick to acquire Brown this offseason.

That said, there's still plenty of season left for Brown to make an impact. The 29-year-old's return to practice is a positive sign. However, there's also a discussion to be had about Brown returning when the Patriots bye week follows their game in Munich. New England might hold off on Brown's return until after their Week 11 bye, giving him an extra two weeks of rest. Based on his practice participation and the fact that he made the trip, all signs point toward Brown playing on Sunday.

At running back, the Patriots could be down their top two backs on Sunday. Along with Henderson being out due to illness, top RB Rhamondre Stevenson is officially questionable after participating in a limited capacity in the two practices in Munich. Early reports indicated that Stevenson would miss games due to his knee injury, so it's a pleasant surprise that the Pats lead back at least has a chance to play on Sunday.

If Stevenson can't play or is limited, third back Corey Kiner figures to get a bulk of the early-down carries. Kiner has shown good burst, vision, and jump-cut ability in limited carries. He's averaging an impressive 4.9 yards per rush and has seven explosive runs (10-plus yards). Kiner has been a nice find and was pushing for more carries even in a healthy backfield. However, Stevenson is also a highly productive back in the passing game, both as a receiver and pass blocker.

The Pats RB1 hauled in a 30-yard touchdown vs. Green Bay last week, creating a mismatch against a linebacker on a wheel route, while Stevenson has almost weekly blocking highlights in blitz protection. To manage Stevenson's knee injury, one option might be to have him play only in passing situations. Along with his ability to execute blocks, the Patriots blitz-protection system is highly complex, so Stevenson at less than 100 percent might be New England's best option, even if it's just in a limited role on passing downs.

New England tried second-year RB Lan Larison in passing situations when Stevenson left the loss to the Packers, and Larison struggled in pass protection (two pressures). If Stevenson is inactive, the Patriots could also elevate practice-squad RB Terrell Jennings. However, Jennings is more of a downhill between-the-tackles runner. So, whether New England's healthy backs can execute in blitz protection is a huge question mark.

Along with the running backs blocking, the Patriots are also tracking toward starting their sixth different offensive line combination through 10 games. Backup G Walter Rouse is working through the NFL's concussion protocol. Rouse still has a chance to play, while the Pats could activate veteran C/G Greg Van Roten from injured reserve, who was a full participant in Friday's practice. New England's most likely starting five is LT Will Campbell, LG Greg Van Roten, C Jared Wilson, RG Matt Pryor, and RT Morgan Moses.

Moving over to the defense, the Patriots are once again shorthanded at cornerback with Davis III (knee) set to miss his fifth game this season. Davis will miss his fifth game of the season due to his injured knee, after missing four games with a neck injury. After being a late scratch last week, the good news is that fourth CB Charles Woods (hamstring) practiced all three days and was a full participant Friday.

Hopefully, Woods's increased workload in practice is a sign he's on track to play vs. the Lions. Woods has mostly been the Patriots top backup at outside corner when Davis or Christian Gonzalez are out. On Sunday, one would think that the Patriots would lean on Gonzalez, Woods, and NCB Marcus Jones, while rookie CB Karon Prunty serves as the fourth cornerback. The Pats could also elevate CB Kindle Vildor from the practice squad as more experienced depth behind its three starting corners.

With the team continuing to manage injuries, the Patriots could activate Gilliam and Van Roten from injured reserve on Saturday. New England has now used five of its eight IR-return designations on WR Mack Hollins, OT Marcus Bryant, Brown, Gilliam, and Van Roten. The Patriots only have three more IR-return spots for the rest of the regular season, with WR Romeo Doubs (shoulder) and G Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) as top return candidates after the Patriots Week 11 bye.

After ruling out three players, the Patriots will likely use practice squad elevations to add roster depth. Depending on Stevenson's status, Jennings could be elevated from the practice squad, as could backup guards Andrew Rupcich or Xavier Newman-Johnson. If the Pats don't need guard or running back depth, Vildor could be an option as well – we'll keep you updated.

The Patriots will then square off against the Lions at Allianz Stadium in Munich on Sunday.

title: NFL midseason superlatives and lessons: Josh Allen for MVP, all-in moves, dashed hopes
description:
With nine weeks of action in the books, the NFL regular season has reached its midway point.
Cousins, now 38 but among the league leaders in passing yards and touchdowns this season, should elevate a Vikings offense with plenty of talented receivers.
The San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs upgraded their wide receiver units by adding Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, respectively.
Scoring holds steady Teams have combined to score 45.93 points per game this season, according to NFL Research.
Superlative check-in MVP — QB Josh Allen, Buffalo Bills It’s a crowded race for the NFL’s highest individual honor.
text:
With nine weeks of action in the books, the NFL regular season has reached its midway point. We’ve learned quite a bit about this year’s teams, players and coaches, and how every piece fits into the puzzle and the ways in which the campaign has taken shape.

A lot can (and will) change between now and the end of Week 18, but by now we have a good idea of who leads the pack, who has some catching up to do and who is all but hopeless.

The NFL never disappoints, and the season’s homestretch will deliver all manner of compelling developments.

Here are some lessons and superlatives so far.

Lessons learned

Nothing is promised

The Los Angeles Rams looked like the team to beat when training camps opened in late July. Hardly anything has gone their way since.

Their trouble started with a disastrous travel plan for the opener in Australia, followed by prized offseason acquisition Myles Garrett’s Week 1 knee injury and surgery, repeated special teams woes and injuries to top wideouts Davante Adams and Puka Nacua. Garrett returned in Week 9 and played like his usual game-wrecking self, but Sean McVay and his 5-4 Rams have a long road to realize their Super Bowl aspirations. Los Angeles has a 41 percent chance of making the postseason, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator.

The Rams aren’t the only projected contender whose plans have gone awry. The Baltimore Ravens lost their top two quarterbacks — Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley — in just over a quarter of their Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills. That led the Ravens to start undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano, himself on a hobbled ankle, against the mighty Jacksonville Jaguars four days later. A disastrous performance pushed Baltimore (4-5) to trade for veteran Jacoby Brissett, with the hope that he can string together some wins in case Jackson returns from thumb surgery for a late playoff push.

Meanwhile, the Philadelphia Eagles envisioned a bounce-back season after last year’s wild-card round exit. But injuries — including Jalen Hurts’ mind-bending blood clot situation — derailed those plans. General manager Howie Roseman has since unloaded veterans for draft picks to facilitate an offseason rebuild.

Drastic times call for drastic measures

The Minnesota Vikings opened the season with a league-best 6-0 record thanks in large part to a dominant defense helmed by coordinator Brian Flores. But the team’s hope that offseason pickup Kyler Murray would settle into coach Kevin O’Connell’s system and direct a good-enough offense never materialized. Then Murray suffered a hamstring injury during the Vikings’ Week 8 loss to the Detroit Lions, and backup Carson Wentz filled in for the next outing with a dismal showing on “Monday Night Football.”

In danger of wasting a championship-caliber defense, the Vikings traded a third-round pick to the Las Vegas Raiders for quarterback Kirk Cousins, who played in Minnesota from 2018 to 2023. Cousins, now 38 but among the league leaders in passing yards and touchdowns this season, should elevate a Vikings offense with plenty of talented receivers. If he and O’Connell can produce a top-10 attack, Minnesota has a legitimate shot at contending for its first Super Bowl.

When within striking distance …

With both conferences wide open, front-runners made aggressive moves before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Most teams, like the Vikings, attempted to improve weak spots on their rosters.

The Jaguars swung big, acquiring defensive playmakers Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III. The San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs upgraded their wide receiver units by adding Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, respectively. The 49ers also brought back Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, while the Seattle Seahawks bolstered their offensive line with guard Quenton Nelson and the Bills addressed their secondary with safety Amani Hooker.

These contenders will continue fine-tuning their lineups in hopes of peaking during the playoffs.

Defense matters

Everyone loves offensive fireworks, but we’ve once again been reminded that it’s hard to win consistently without a quality defense. The Dallas Cowboys have one of the NFL’s best offenses, but their inability to stop opposing teams has left them with a 4-5 record and a 32 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to The Athletic’s projections. The 4-5 Raiders (7 percent chance to make the postseason) have a similar profile.

In fact, all 15 of the NFL’s worst scoring defenses have losing records.

Scoring holds steady

Teams have combined to score 45.93 points per game this season, according to NFL Research. That’s down slightly from 46.74 points per game halfway through last season, and a tick higher than the 45.36 points per game after nine weeks in 2024.

Down to the wire

The league has seen plenty of close finishes this season. Through nine weeks, 77 games have come down to one score (eight or fewer points). That ties the 2016 season for the third-most through Week 9 in NFL history, trailing only the 2024 (79) and 2022 (79) seasons.

Of those 77 games, 41 have featured a game-winning score in the final five minutes of regulation or overtime. That’s the second-most through Week 9, trailing only the 2021 season, which featured 42 such finishes. In 25 games, the winning team rallied from at least 10 points down, which ties the 2011 season for the fourth-most in league history. That figure trails the 1987 (30), 2020 (26) and 2022 (26) seasons.

Special teams spike

The NFL implemented its “dynamic kickoff” before the 2024 season to help the play regain relevance after years of teams booming the ball out of the end zone and settling for touchbacks rather than risking big returns.

The changes have seemingly done the trick, as the number of kickoff returns (1,118) and kickoff return yards (28,896) mark the most in league history through nine weeks.

Superlative check-in

MVP — QB Josh Allen, Buffalo Bills

It’s a crowded race for the NFL’s highest individual honor. Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow has bounced back from last year’s injury-plagued campaign, leading the league with 298.3 passing yards per game and 23 passing touchdowns against six interceptions. He also ranks first in passer rating (114.8) and completion percentage (74.0) among quarterbacks who’ve thrown at least 100 passes.

Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love is also playing the best ball of his career, averaging 290.9 passing yards per game (second) with 19 touchdown passes (third), a 97.9 passer rating and six interceptions. And how about 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy? The 2022 Mr. Irrelevant has been anything but, with 247.5 passing yards per game, 17 touchdown passes, a 109.8 passer rating, a 69.1 percent completion rate and five interceptions for the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers.

All of those signal callers deserve recognition, but Allen carries the Bills and impacts opposing defenses in ways no other quarterback can. Averaging 253.4 passing yards with 12 touchdown passes, six interceptions and nine rushing touchdowns, Allen has led Buffalo to a 7-1 start while pacing an offense that averages a league-high 32.0 points a game and masking the struggles of a defense that yields 330.4 yards and 23.4 points per contest.

Offensive player of the year — QB Joe Burrow, Cincinnati Bengals

Burrow appears on pace to win the passing title, and despite competition from running backs Jahmyr Gibbs (847 rushing yards, nine touchdowns) and Bijan Robinson (880 rushing yards, five touchdowns), Burrow feels like the most deserving choice.

Defensive player of the year — Edge Will Anderson Jr., Houston Texans

The fourth-year pro leads the league with 9.5 sacks and is on pace to shatter his career-best mark of 12. Also making strong cases for themselves: linebacker Fred Warner (77 tackles, five forced fumbles) and defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons (48 tackles, six sacks, six pass breakups and 11 quarterback hits).

Offensive rookie of the year — WR Denzel Boston, Cleveland Browns

We’ll see what kind of numbers and impact quarterback Fernando Mendoza delivers over the final eight games, but Boston gets the nod for now, thanks to his 32 catches, 507 yards and three touchdowns.

Defensive rookie of the year – LB Arvell Reese, New York Giants

The No. 5 pick in the 2026 NFL Draft has racked up 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for loss, 49 solo tackles (68 total), a forced fumble and an interception for the surprising Giants.

Coach of the Year — John Harbaugh, New York Giants

Ben Johnson continues to lead an impressive Chicago Bears team, and Kyle Shanahan’s 49ers rank among the Super Bowl favorites.

But with the Giants unexpectedly leading their division and contending for their first playoff berth since the 2022 season — with a backup quarterback, no less — Harbaugh gets the nod.

Comeback Player of the Year — Patrick Mahomes, Kansas City Chiefs

The two-time league MVP and three-time Super Bowl champion adds more hardware to his collection. He’s made a seamless return from a torn ACL and LCL to lead the Chiefs back to contention.

text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- The Baltimore Ravens say Lamar Jackson's dislocated and broken right thumb has a typical recovery timeline of six to 10 weeks, with a source telling ESPN the quarterback has undergone surgery for the injury.

Ravens coach Jesse Minter addressed Jackson's status in a statement released by the team Friday in which he said recovery timelines are "challenging to predict."

"He is doing everything he can to get back, and we will let his progress guide the timing of his return," Minter said. "We are committed to playing our best football over the second half of the season."

With nine weeks remaining in the regular season, Jackson could come back as early as Week 16 against the Cleveland Browns. If Jackson needs 10 weeks to recover, a return would come in the postseason.

The Ravens (4-5) have lost four straight games but are one game out of the final playoff spot in the AFC. Baltimore's playoff chances are projected at 3.7%, according to ESPN Analytics.

To help keep the team's postseason hopes alive, the Ravens traded for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, who is set to start Monday night in Baltimore against the winless Los Angeles Chargers.

Jackson hurt his right thumb on the first play of a 36-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills on Nov. 1. His right hand hit the arm of Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau while trying to throw a pass.

This is the second significant injury this season for Jackson, who missed three games with a high ankle sprain. He has played only 14 full quarters.

The Ravens have usually struggled without Jackson. With Jackson as its starting quarterback, Baltimore is 82-38 (.683), including playoffs, and averages 27.6 points per game. Without Jackson as their starter since 2019, the Ravens are 7-15 (.318), including the postseason, and average 17.3 points per game.

text:
Joey Porter Jr. made it clear this week that his recent absences are due to injury, not contract issues.

"I don't even know where that narrative come from," the Dallas cornerback said Thursday, via ESPN. "I get it. It's the internet, but I really don't pay no attention to that or really care for that. My goal is to win games and play football, and that's what I want to do. So if there's any chance I could get on the field, I'm going to get on the field and do what I do best."

Porter joined the Cowboys following a trade from Pittsburgh ahead of Week 4 against Houston, when he first suffered a nagging ankle injury. He missed Week 5 against Tampa Bay due to a severe illness before returning for the next three games. He was inactive for last week’s win over the Colts due to the ankle/foot issue.

The 26-year-old sat out in Pittsburgh early this season due to a contract standoff, with reported back pain. That situation is coloring the current one with the Cowboys. However, Porter insists the two scenarios are completely different, noting his “whole foot is jacked up.”

"Just to be able to run, be able to cut," Porter said. "I play a position where I got to guard the most athletic people on the field, so if I can't run, skip or jump, then I'm no use out there."

The corner has not practiced this week. The question is whether he can do enough Friday to be ready for Sunday’s bout against the San Francisco 49ers.

"It's definitely frustrating. I'm on a new team and I want to show these guys what I can do, and I feel like I have been for the most part when I'm on the field," Porter said. "It's frustrating for everybody. I'm just trying to keep the main thing the main thing and get back as fast as possible to play with the guys."

The New York Giants' loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night helped the Cowboys' playoff chances considerably. Dallas now sits 1.5 games back in the NFC East race.

What's more, head coach Sean McVay said his expectation is Nacua will miss "extended time."
Losing Nacua is quite the blow for Los Angeles seeing how Davante Adams is already sidelined with a hamstring injury.
Ultimately, the Rams are not going to be nearly as dangerous with both Nacua and Adams out.
The Green Bay Packers have the final wild-card spot at 6-3 and will face the Rams in Week 12 while Nacua is still out.
text:
The Los Angeles Rams will be without wide receiver Puka Nacua for the foreseeable future.

The NFC West team placed the playmaker on injured reserve because of his MCL injury. What's more, head coach Sean McVay said his expectation is Nacua will miss "extended time."

This is a change in direction for the Rams, as McVay initially told reporters that even though the wide receiver was going to miss "a significant period of time," the plan was not to place him on IR due to "semantics with the roster."

Losing Nacua is quite the blow for Los Angeles seeing how Davante Adams is already sidelined with a hamstring injury.

Nacua's injury happened during Sunday's win over the Washington Commanders, although he still finished with a head-turning 14 receptions for 150 yards and one touchdown on 19 targets. Through seven games this season, he has 70 catches for 715 yards and four touchdowns.

With both of Matthew Stafford's top receivers sidelined, the Rams will likely rely on the combination of Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield and CJ Daniels at the position. Tight end Tyler Higbee will likely see plenty of targets as well, although even he missed practice Thursday because of an illness.

Ultimately, the Rams are not going to be nearly as dangerous with both Nacua and Adams out.

Nacua is one of the best wide receivers in the league and someone Stafford routinely targets double-digit amounts of time per game. There will be more pressure on the rushing attack to carry the offense with the two top playmakers sidelined, and there is also little room for error in the NFC standings.

After all, Los Angeles is three games behind the San Francisco 49ers in the NFC West at 5-4 and on the outside of the playoff picture looking in at this point. The Green Bay Packers have the final wild-card spot at 6-3 and will face the Rams in Week 12 while Nacua is still out.

With remaining games against the Packers, 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs, as well as two against the Seattle Seahawks, there is a real chance the Rams will miss the playoffs.

text:
Despite a season-ending injury to promising rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton, general manager John Lynch and the 49ers decided not to bolster their defensive front at Tuesday's NFL trade deadline.

With the addition of DeForest Buckner one week before, Lynch explained in an interview with KNBR's "Murph and Markus" Thursday that he's confident with San Francisco's defensive line as it is currently constructed and opted not to make any deals to add to the position group.

"If you've seen our history, I think that's always a spot -- you can't have enough good D-linemen," Lynch told Brian Murphy and Markus Boucher. "Now you do have a 53-man roster, too, and so, there's only so much you can do. But, we did make some calls. We inquired, but we really like our group."

Lynch noted Buckner, Osa Odhigizuwa, Nick Bosa, rookie Romello Height, Keion White, Mykel Williams and CJ West as key players on the defensive line. The 49ers have focused on bolstering the group through the draft, free agency and trade acquisition, and the team feels content with that depth allowing them all to rotate in and out to keep them fresh.

But, the 49ers have not been able to record many sacks this season. Their total of 15 sacks are the fifth-fewest in the NFL this season. San Francisco has not recorded a sack in their last two games.

Lynch notes that sacks are not the end-all, be-all metric for measuring defensive-line success.

"I think a lot of people might have some concern the last couple weeks; not a ton of sacks," Lynch admitted. "I would tell you that the game plans in those games, [then-Las Vegas Raiders quarterback] Kirk [Cousins] was getting rid of the ball really quick. We had like nine tackles for losses in that game. So, our group was doing some damage.

San Francisco 49ers

Find the latest San Francisco 49ers news, highlights, analysis and more with NBC Sports Bay Area and California.

"And then when he held the ball, we were in his face. And so, I like where our pass rush is at. I think we'll finish at the quarterback the rest of the season, and I think we have ample assets in that group to go race them."

The defensive line wreaked havoc on the Raiders' rushing attack and allowed just 24 rushing yards, a season-best for the 49ers. They also recorded a season-high nine tackles for loss, as Lynch mentioned.

Lynch also believes that the defensive front's efficiency showed up in forcing three interceptions. And just because the sack total is low so far, it does not necessarily mean that trend will continue.

"You want to bring the quarterback down, but pressures are key ... they lead to turnovers," Lynch explained. "I would tell you that we were kind of at the bottom in turnovers and we had five and we've worked our way up. So, it can change really quickly.

"I've got a lot of belief in this defensive front and their ability to play at a high level and create chaos and things of that nature. I think we really believe in this group, so we think that will come."

The 49ers' defensive line will have their next challenge in Week 10 against the Dallas Cowboys, who have allowed just 14 sacks this season, the eighth-fewest in the NFL.

LOS ANGELES — The Los Angeles Rams are placing star wide receiver Puka Nacua on injured reserve after all. They announced the move on Thursday. Nacua must now miss at least the next four games.

The team signed wide receiver Brennan Presley from the practice squad to fill the roster spot. It also signed wide receiver Tyler Scott to the practice squad.

The move comes four days after Nacua sprained his MCL and PCL and suffered turf toe on his 16th and final touch in a 20-13 victory over the Washington Commanders. Coach Sean McVay said Wednesday that Nacua would miss significant time, but that he would not go on IR due to “roster semantics.”

Teams can bring back eight players from IR during the season, and it’s becoming likely that Nacua will be the Rams’ seventh, leaving just one more.

The Rams have already used three of them on defensive end Myles Garrett, rookie tackle Keagen Trost and running back Ronnie Rivers. Tight end Terrance Ferguson is expected to be the fourth once he recovers from the hamstring injury he suffered last week, which should keep him out for a couple more weeks.

The Rams have until Nov. 25 to activate Ferguson if they want him to return this season.

Defensive end Kobie Turner and wide receiver Davante Adams are expected to be the fifth and sixth returns. If Nacua follows them, that would leave the Rams with just one spot left to return a player in the regular season. Teams do gain two additional return spots if they make the postseason.

Without Nacua or Adams on Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals, the Rams will look to a wide receiver room of Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, CJ Daniels, Xavier Smith and Presley.

After facing Arizona, the Rams will enter their bye before games against the Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers, all of which Nacua will miss.

The Rams opted not to add a wide receiver at Tuesday’s trade deadline, believing Adams and Ferguson would return soon to bolster the passing game and that Nacua could return later this season.

text:
FRISCO, Texas -- Dallas Cowboys cornerback Joey Porter Jr. wants it known that his absence from the field the past two weeks has everything to do with an ankle injury and nothing to do with him worrying about a future contract.

"I don't even know where that narrative come from," Porter said. "I get it. It's the internet, but I really don't pay no attention to that or really care for that. My goal is to win games and play football, and that's what I want to do. So if there's any chance I could get on the field, I'm going to get on the field and do what I do best."

Porter was inactive last week on the road against the Indianapolis Colts and was unable to finish the loss to the Arizona Cardinals because of an ankle injury he initially suffered Oct. 4 against the Houston Texans in his first game with the Cowboys following the trade from the Pittsburgh Steelers.

On Thursday, Porter did not practice for the second straight day, but he worked on the resistance cords during the portion of practice open to the media Thursday. He said he did some running and felt confident.

He hopes to do more Friday with an eye on playing Sunday against the visiting San Francisco 49ers.

"Just to be able to run, be able to cut," Porter said. "I play a position where I got to guard the most athletic people on the field, so if I can't run, skip or jump, then I'm no use out there."

Dallas coach Brian Schottenheimer said Porter is dealing with a heel issue accompanied by the ankle.

"The whole foot's jacked up," Porter said. "I was playing on it for a while, and it just kept getting worse to where I had to shut it down. I feel like all the guys are wanting me to get back. They know what I could do when I'm out there on the field. I bring a presence out there that is a game-changing type presence. I'm just trying to get back out there as fast as possible."

The Cowboys acquired Porter from the Steelers on Oct. 1 for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. He has played three full games, missing the Oct. 8 meeting against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with an illness.

He is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent when the season ends.

"It's definitely frustrating. I'm on a new team and I want to show these guys what I can do, and I feel like I have been for the most part when I'm on the field," Porter said. "... It's frustrating for everybody. I'm just trying to keep the main thing the main thing and get back as fast as possible to play with the guys."

The Denver Broncos agreed to trade a 2027 fourth-round draft pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Los Angeles Chargers in exchange for linebacker Daiyan Henley ahead of the NFL's trade deadline on Tuesday afternoon, pending a physical.

Then, late Wednesday evening, the Broncos announced that the trade would not be finalized. We now know the details of why the trade fell through.

Denver "discovered an issue" with one of Henley's knees during his physical at the team's facility on Wednesday, according to ESPN's Jeff Legwold. Despite that "issue," the Broncos still wanted to trade for Henley, but on revised terms.

In place of the original fourth- and fifth-round picks, Denver's revised offers were either a fourth-rounder and a seventh-rounder, or a fourth-rounder and another pick flip, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. L.A. was not interested in either option and the trade fell through.

When the NFL's transaction wire is released later today, the unprocessed trade will be designated as a "failed physical." But the Chargers apparently feel more confident in Henley's knee than the Broncos, so the linebacker could go right back to playing when he returns to L.A. this week.

text:
MUNICH (AP) — Heading into international games, NFL coaches typically talk up the niceties of “growing the game” globally.

Not this week.

The New England Patriots (5-4) have lost two of their past three games and have a slew of injury concerns, including running back Rhamondre Stevenson. The Detroit Lions, even with a 6-2 record and four straight victories, are trying to keep pace in the tight NFC North.

Sunday's game in Munich is a big one for both teams.

Lions coach Dan Campbell wasn't focused on the international implications.

“Well, if I’m being honest, I just haven’t thought that far into it. I’m like, ‘We’ve got to get prepared,’” Campbell said.

The Patriots were embarrassed at home by the Green Bay Packers last week, losing 45-27, with Drake Maye throwing three interceptions and the secondary struggling to contain the Packers passing game.

Campbell expects a much-improved New England team on Sunday.

“You look at the totality of what this team is capable of, the firepower they have, and they’re a good team. They’re dangerous,” he said. “And they’re going to clean a lot of things up.”

The Lions slogged through a 19-9 win over the rebuilding Miami Dolphins last week, relying on four field goals from Jake Bates. It was also just one week after a neck injury to All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell.

Detroit's bye week is in the rearview mirror and after Munich the team will host Tampa Bay and then Chicago on Thanksgiving Day.

“It's a good thing to be tested during the season,” Campbell said. "It really is. And to have to go through some of these tough stretches because that’s what the playoffs are. That’s what it is. And certainly if you got to go on the road. So, that’s what this is. This is about us. This is the next obstacle we have. Told the team we’re not going to clear it. Our objective is to go through it and that’s the mindset.”

Injuries are a top concern for New England. Before traveling Wednesday night, the Patriots ruled out LG Ben Brown (knee), CB Carlton Davis III (knee) and RB TreVeyon Henderson (illness).

Stevenson, the team's leading rusher with 399 yards on 102 carries, didn't practice Wednesday because of a knee injury.

That could put second-year running back Corey Kiner in line for the bulk of the carries.

“Corey has done a really nice job, but there are also some things that Corey has to be able to improve on,” coach Mike Vrabel said, citing "recognition of the pressure and then the ability to block the pressure.”

The coach said “a lot of contending teams” are 5-4.

“We’ve got to start putting ourselves in position to play meaningful games in January or in the middle of January,” Vrabel said. “It’s usually what happens in the National Football League; a bunch of teams get bunched up and they go in different directions, and I know the direction that we’re going to head in, and that’s going to be the one that’s forward, positive and winning.”

Need to know

New England (5-4) vs. Detroit (6-2) in Munich, Germany.

When/where to watch: Sunday, 9:30 a.m. EST, FOX

Latest odds: Lions by 2 1/2

Against the spread: Patriots 3-5-1; Lions 4-4

Last week: Patriots lost to Packers 45-27; Lions beat Dolphins 19-9

Last meeting: Patriots won 29-0 on Oct. 9, 2022, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass.

Series record: Patriots lead 8-5

Matchup to watch

Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez against Lions receivers Jameson Williams and Amon-Ra St. Brown. Gonzalez, who signed a lucrative contract extension in September, is hoping to bounce back from struggling against Green Bay last week. According to the NFL Next Gen Stats, he gave up 105 yards to Matthew Golden and 82 yards to Christian Watson. St. Brown, who typically lines up in the slot, leads the Lions with 61 receptions for 657 yards. He’s scored five touchdowns. Williams has 468 yards on 28 receptions — though just one last week in Miami — and five TDs.

Stats and stuff

— Detroit running back Jahmyr Gibbs leads the NFL with 60 scrimmage touchdowns (48 rushing, 12 receiving) and ranks second with 6,161 scrimmage yards since entering the NFL in 2023.

— With a touchdown Sunday, Gibbs can tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Terrell Davis (61 touchdowns) for the most touchdowns by a player in his first four seasons in NFL history.

— This is Detroit's first international game since 2015. The Lions are 1-1 internationally.

— The Patriots won three international games with Tom Brady at quarterback. They lost 32-16 to Jacksonville in London in 2024 in Drake Maye's second NFL start; and lost 10-6 to the Colts in Frankfurt in 2023 with Mac Jones at the helm.

— Entering Week 10, Maye is tied with Justin Herbert for most interceptions (11). He's tied for fourth in touchdown passes (18).

text:
Chris Olave has experienced so many frightening collisions during his NFL career that fans have started joking he needs to wear multiple helmets just to make it through an entire football game. Since joining the New Orleans Saints in 2022, Olave has established himself as one of the league’s most talented young receivers through his exceptional route running, impressive hands, and ability to create separation against elite defensive backs. However, his professional career has also featured repeated concussions and dangerous collisions that have raised legitimate concerns about his long-term health. Watching a talented receiver repeatedly suffer injuries is especially frustrating because his ability to produce spectacular offensive highlights remains undeniable whenever he’s healthy.

What makes Olave’s situation particularly concerning is how seriously repeated head injuries must be treated in professional football. During the 2024 season, he suffered a concussion after a collision against the Carolina Panthers, adding to an injury history that had already interrupted his development. Although the idea of wearing multiple helmets is obviously a joke rather than a realistic medical solution, it reflects the concern fans feel whenever Olave takes another dangerous hit. His early career included consecutive 1,000-yard receiving seasons, demonstrating the extraordinary talent that made him a first-round draft selection. However, maintaining his health is far more important than any individual receiving statistic or highlight. Olave’s experiences illustrate why player safety and appropriate concussion management remain essential issues throughout professional football.

Deshaun Watson (concussion): Watson will start Sunday against the Houston Texans. His expected return is a significant development for Cleveland, with the quarterback set to get back into the lineup after dealing with a concussion.

Jared Goff (chest): Goff was listed as a limited participant on Wednesday's practice report. The Detroit Lions quarterback's workload will be worth monitoring as the week progresses. It is unlikely that Goff will miss a week, though.

Gardner Minshew, Kyler Murray and Malik Willis injury news

Gardner Minshew (elbow): Minshew will undergo surgery and miss the remainder of the season, according to head coach Mike LaFleur. The injury ends his 2026 campaign and leaves his team without him for the rest of the year.

Kyler Murray (hamstring): Murray remains week-to-week, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell. The quarterback does not have a definitive return date, leaving his availability uncertain. It might not matter now anyway, as Kirk Cousins is expected to be the starter, and maybe even as early as this weekend.

The move will sideline the quarterback for at least four games, creating another significant change to Miami's quarterback situation. In a season that was already a lost one, Miami is likely going to struggle even more.

title: Inside the physical and mental toll of Malik Nabers' knee injury - ESPN
authors: Jordan Raanan, Jamison Hensley, Daniel Oyefusi, Jordan Reid, NFL Nation, Dan Graziano, Jeremy Fowler, Bill Barnwell, Courtney Cronin, Ben Baby
description:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had a conversation with his uncle before training camp in 2025.
"I kind of lost myself in the process," Nabers said while opening up about his rehab for the first time.
This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place.
Together, they monitored the wide receiver's rehab, and early on in the process, Nabers needed the mental boost.
The wide receiver is admittedly in a better place but wouldn't say he's happy with what he has accomplished so far.
text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had a conversation with his uncle before training camp in 2025. His uncle was asking about his nephew's journey to NFL stardom, when he became a Pro Bowl player while setting a Giants record with 109 receptions during his rookie season.

Nabers, the sixth overall pick out of LSU in 2024, told him how he didn't view his journey as all that hard. In fact, it came relatively easy for the wide receiver while compiling 1,204 yards and seven touchdowns despite playing with four quarterbacks in 2024. Nabers noted there were a lot of other players who had gone through "way harder things."

Little did he know what was coming.

Fast forward to three months later in Week 4 of the 2025 season against the Los Angeles Chargers, with Nabers lying on the MetLife Stadium turf reaching for his right knee. He had jumped to make a catch deep down the right sideline and knew immediately, in midair, that something was wrong.

The Giants' young playmaker tore the ACL and meniscus in his right knee.

This was the test he subconsciously knew was coming even if it was one he hadn't asked for.

On Nov. 1, 2026, Nabers is standing in the middle of the Giants' locker room seemingly fully back after four straight 100-yard receiving games, answering questions about the emotional challenge that came with the serious knee injury that cost him most of last season.

Nabers revealed to ESPN prior to the first-place Giants' matchup Thursday night with the Washington Commanders (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime) details about that private conversation with his uncle that left the wide receiver once upon a time thinking his journey wouldn't be that formidable.

"Kind of ... kind of just ... and then this happened," Nabers reminisced last week. "And I was like, OK, well, this is the challenge that I said I never had. It's an opportunity to get back from a challenge and see how I can come back off of it."

Nabers found out the physical and mental toll recovering from such a significant injury would entail ups and downs in the process, everything from lack of flexion in his knee to a second "cleanup" procedure to eliminate stiffness.

The original thought from the Giants was that he would be back in the spring. Then even the summer and training camp was in doubt.

"He had a slow comeback process just due to the severity of his injury," said Dr. Sharif "Reef" Tabbah, a physical therapist who worked with Nabers in Miami earlier this year.

Nabers tried hard to keep his faith, believing and telling himself everything was going to be fine when, in reality, he had no idea. The thoughts were bouncing like a ping pong ball off a wall, volleyed away but returning with a vengeance.

"He was definitely struggling. You could tell he was struggling with the process," said Giants coach John Harbaugh, who was hired in January. "He even told me he was never hurt before, how hard it was. I think every little up and down in the process would really affect him emotionally, mentally, whatever."

Nabers was going through an internal battle during a long and hard rehab. Through it all, he was trying to find himself. There were days when he was searching for answers but couldn't find them. He would have to figure out where and when they would come from. It wasn't going to be easy.

"I kind of lost myself in the process," Nabers said while opening up about his rehab for the first time.

NABERS' INJURY HISTORY prior to the Giants was not extensive. There was a shoulder injury that forced him to miss a couple of games at LSU his freshman season. He had some problems with his toe in New York, but nothing major. No long-term injuries or extended periods out of football.

This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place.

"Just my attitude," Nabers said of why he lost himself. "Everybody didn't know what my mindset was. Just at a loss for words. Didn't really have a lot of words to say. Didn't really have, I don't know, I kind of was empty. Just didn't know what the future holds, how I was going to respond, just with everything that was going on. Everybody just didn't know."

There were days when his knee swelled, when it was stiff and didn't bend. His progress, if it was outlined in a graph, might resemble the stock market during its most volatile month.

This sent Nabers into a tailspin. He was fighting himself.

"My mind was just all over the place. I didn't really understand and didn't really want to communicate well," he said. "Just didn't know how to communicate how I was feeling and how things were going because every day it was something new. ... So I just didn't know, I just didn't really see a process. I didn't really see progress from week to week."

Nabers said he didn't lean on anyone in particular, not even Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, one of his closest friends -- who also spent this past offseason combating an injury-plagued season. He was around Giants running back Cam Skattebo a bunch as they both rehabbed injuries -- Skattebo suffered an open fracture to his right leg in October of last year and still ultimately returned for the start of mandatory minicamp before Nabers. But Nabers kept to himself. He didn't feel like sharing.

"When he was in that deep place, I was in that deep place, too. We were both together," Skattebo said. "We were both in that same spot as not being able to say anything, not being able to express ourselves. ... He wasn't seeing the progress that he wanted but as he kept going and up until now, he's starting to feel that progress that's being made."

In a way, it was an extension of Nabers' nature. He is generally a quiet guy.

"When you go through an internal battle with yourself you start to figure out what you need better than other people telling you what you need when they don't know you," Nabers said. "... You start finding more about yourself that you didn't know yet. ... So I just went through it myself."

RECOVERY FROM A torn ACL can be a beast. Adding a full meniscus repair only adds to the difficulty.

It's why Nabers was still walking with crutches and wearing a brace in January, some two-plus months after the surgery was performed by Dallas Cowboys head team physician Daniel E. Cooper -- a renowned doctor known for recently operating on other NFL players such as Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and Las Vegas Raiders tight end Brock Bowers. Typically, full meniscus repair adds to the recovery timeline. It turned out to be the case for Nabers, who almost didn't play Week 1 roughly a year after his injury.

"His rehab protocol was a little bit slow," Tabbah said. "He had a lot of limitations still with mobility and strength and tolerance of functional exercises and things like that. So we were in that phase of ... tolerating different functional movement patterns and trying to get him ready to progress to that later stage."

Dr. Reef, as he is known, is a doctor of physical therapy and certified strength and conditioning specialist who founded Alkeme Sports RX in South Florida. He has worked with a long list of professional athletes, including Commanders wide receiver Stephon Diggs last year as he rehabbed from a torn ACL.

Dr. Reef worked with Nabers in Florida for most of February through May. He admitted it was a "challenging rehab case." But, along with new Giants trainer Adam Bennett, they together a plan that would be best for Nabers' healing. Together, they monitored the wide receiver's rehab, and early on in the process, Nabers needed the mental boost.

"I just try to give them reassurance and just let them know, 'Hey, this will pass. I know this is tough right now, but this is where you are today. It's not where you're going to be in months to come,'" Dr. Reef said. "I know this is your first rodeo when it comes to dealing with something like this, but it's not mine."

It was Dr. Reef's 15th season working with athletes. Diggs' ability to return to the field strong last season was a selling point Tabbah noted. He also kept reminding Nabers his process was different from everyone else's and warned against Nabers comparing himself to others because no injury is the same. Each comes with its own complexities.

It was when Nabers was back working with the Giants in the spring when significant strides were made. He had a second procedure in early spring, considered a cleanup to remove scar tissue and decrease stiffness.

"We had gone on the field, done a little bit of some footwork. We had done some bag work a little bit," Dr. Reef said. "And then every time we'd make some progress, he'd get a flare up and we'd go backwards. So that's when we eventually said, 'Hey, let's get this thing cleaned out.'"

Nabers then began making significant progress late in the spring/early in the summer working with rehabilitation and return-to-play coordinator Allison Boudtrou and the Giants' medical staff. He spent a good chunk of his summer getting well in New Jersey.

The end was in sight.

The Giants thought it was important for Nabers to get on the field this summer. They decided not to have him start on the physically unable to perform list. It was important for Nabers to do what he could to get over both the physical and mental humps.

Even when he wasn't able to do much physical movement in the spring, the Giants were managing his mind as much as his body. Wide receivers coach Chad Hall made him go through walk-throughs just to get his focus off the weight of rehab.

Nabers wanted to start by learning one position in the new offense. Hall and the Giants said no. They wanted to give him more to keep him occupied and ready. They were managing his mindset.

"Challenge him in different ways so he can focus more on [the football] stuff," Hall said.

That is where Nabers thrives -- playing football. It's where he wanted to be and the Giants were working to get him there.

NABERS WAS ON the field practicing at the start of this season's training camp. Considering where he was a few months earlier, it's hardly a surprise that he said his "soul came back to life," after practicing in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. He was ready for the season opener against the Dallas Cowboys despite legitimate uncertainty about whether he would actually play.

Finally in his happy place. No longer lost. Still waiting for the breakthrough.

"I guess I'm still waiting for that moment," Nabers said.

Even though he looks good and the production is there, the star wide receiver believes there is still more progress to be made mentally and physically. Nabers was insistent the first few weeks of the 2026 season that he was "rusty." He was slipping coming out of routes and still learning to trust the right knee.

Then he had a stretch of four straight 100-yard games that ended Sunday in Week 9 at Philadelphia. He currently ranks 11th in the NFL with 648 receiving yards on 53 catches.

It seems Nabers, who took offense this week to Fox broadcaster Greg Olsen's comments about his body language, is back to his pre-injury form. But don't tell him that.

"Working on it," he said. "Working on it."

The biggest thing he has learned is patience. Nabers also still believes there's more to go physically. He feels he can get stronger and improve flexion in the knee. But there's likely always going to be a next level he's looking to reach.

The wide receiver is admittedly in a better place but wouldn't say he's happy with what he has accomplished so far.

In his mind, the comeback is not yet complete.

title: Jalen Hurts played through pain. Why do we keep celebrating it? - The Athletic
authors: Katrina Monton, Elise Devlin and Reuben Pinder
description:
Last month, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts sought treatment for a calf injury.
Hurts is now expected to miss the remainder of the season, though the team anticipates a full recovery.
In 2023, he continued competing through a knee injury, and the following season, he played with a broken finger.
What I keep coming back to is this: We assume pushing athletes beyond their limits produces excellence, but what if that approach is actually holding them back?
Once we knew Hurts was more seriously injured and had blood clots in both lungs, Robinson apologized for his comments.
text:
This story is part of Peak, The Athletic’s desk covering the mental side of sports. Sign up for Peak’s newsletter here.

Katrina Monton is an organizational psychologist and professor at Rutgers University. She also played water polo for Team Canada, winning a silver medal at the 2009 World Championships.

Last month, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts sought treatment for a calf injury. He practiced in the days following the injury and, before the Eagles’ next game in London, was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his leg. Doctors determined that he could safely compete, and so he did.

Further testing revealed a more serious condition: a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in both lungs. Hurts is now expected to miss the remainder of the season, though the team anticipates a full recovery.

In the past, Hurts has been admired for his willingness to push through injuries and adversity. In 2023, he continued competing through a knee injury, and the following season, he played with a broken finger. His ability to compete through pain has earned praise from coaches and teammates, with head coach Nick Sirianni saying Hurts “can play through anything,” and teammate Jordan Mailata describing him as a warrior.

As a former elite athlete and now an organizational psychologist, I see this as more than a single unfortunate incident; it’s a moment that invites us to think about how elite sport normalizes pain, rewards self-sacrifice and too often puts performance ahead of athletes’ health.

I’ve seen this mentality throughout professional sport, and I’ve experienced it myself.

When I made Canada’s national water polo team, I was 14. I then spent almost 15 years competing on the international stage. There was this idea that we were expected to show up ready to train, compete and put everything else on the backburner. It didn’t matter if we were injured, sick or had something going on in our personal lives.

We all knew how replaceable we were.

On the national team, I took pride in my ability to push through whatever was happening in my life. I wore that toughness as a badge of honor, and it became attached to my identity and how I understood myself.

It made me feel I had earned my place on the team.

Most of us who grew up in the 1990s and early 2000s were surrounded by slogans exhorting this mentality: No pain, no gain. No days off. Win at all costs.

So when I suffered a concussion near the end of my career, the pressure to quickly return didn’t need to come from anyone else. By then, years of competing in an environment that celebrated and rewarded toughness and pushing through pain had taught me to expect the same of myself.

We were less than four months away from the Olympic qualifier in 2016. I got hit in the face with the ball at very close range. I was so disoriented and dazed that I actually swam into our own net.

I went to the side of the pool and tried to shake it off. I remember telling our trainer: “I’m good, I’m good.” There was some pride in that response.

I finished training that morning and came back that evening for a scrimmage. It wasn’t until I finished weight training the next day that I felt so nauseous that I nearly vomited. Even then, I thought: Must have the flu!

Eventually, I returned to competition even though I was experiencing pretty frequent headaches.

It’s a very strange attitude to explain. It was like I wasn’t thinking about my own body and my own symptoms. It was just programmed in me.

Looking back, I can question that mentality in a way I wasn’t able to at the time. Now I think: I wonder what that recovery would have looked like if I hadn’t spent years absorbing those messages from coaches, teammates and a broader society that celebrated and rewarded pushing through pain.

I’ve since dedicated my career to understanding how these expectations can undermine the very excellence they try to achieve.

What I keep coming back to is this: We assume pushing athletes beyond their limits produces excellence, but what if that approach is actually holding them back? If we respected those limits instead of overriding them, could we unlock levels of performance we haven’t even begun to imagine?

In my own research with retired Olympic athletes, many participants described pressures very similar to what I experienced. They feared that disclosing an injury or expressing vulnerability could jeopardize their spot on the team. One athlete recalled seeking medical treatment outside her team’s healthcare system because she was afraid that revealing that injury might end her career. Other participants I interviewed talked about skipping MRIs and competing on broken bones.

The problem isn’t athletes who tough it out. It’s the culture of sport that makes speaking up and being honest about your injuries so costly.

We tend to celebrate winning at all costs, even if we may not realize we’re doing it. We treat pushing through pain as proof of commitment. And the stakes are so high. An injury can jeopardize playing time or a spot on the team, which can impact an athlete’s livelihood.

I read an article after Hurts was initially sidelined with the blood clot diagnosis. A former NFL player, Michael Robinson, suggested on NFL Network that Hurts was using his injury to distance himself from the Eagles’ struggling season, even encouraging viewers to compare a superficial blood clot with a “real” one.

Once we knew Hurts was more seriously injured and had blood clots in both lungs, Robinson apologized for his comments. But I think his initial reaction is revealing. It reinforces the belief that athletes are expected to push through pain, and when they can’t, their toughness, commitment and willingness to put their team first are called into question.

I’m not in the business of reducing or removing challenges. That’s why sports are so captivating and powerful. But teams and organizations can create better environments for athletes to have more open and honest conversations. We can do right by the athlete and right by the situation.

When I had my concussion, the conversations I remember having with doctors and coaches were almost entirely about what I needed to do to get back in the pool. There was little discussion about my long-term health, the potential consequences of returning too soon, or even what I wanted. The focus was on getting me back to competition. I still experience migraines today.

I’ve often wondered what it would have been like if we’d had a more open and honest conversation: I really want to play, and I really want to get back, but what does that look like? What should I be comfortable pushing through, and what shouldn’t I? What are the potential consequences for my health, not just now, but years down the road?

Through my work with Speed Skating Canada, which has won more Olympic medals than any other summer or winter Canadian sport, I received a front-row seat to these kinds of changes.

They wanted their athletes to be vocal. They said: We want people to be leaders, to be thinkers, to be pushing back and challenging us.

It’s a true collaboration when it’s done well. In subsequent research, athletes described feeling comfortable raising concerns, sharing doubts and telling coaches when something wasn’t working for them.

And they still won.

We should all be asking not only what athletes are willing to sacrifice for success but whether those sacrifices are necessary, what they cost and why we so rarely recognize the courage it takes to prioritize one’s health.

The next time we celebrate an athlete for being a warrior, we might also consider what we’re asking of the human being behind that performance.

text:
The San Francisco 49ers' convincing 38-17 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders came with a devastating cost. Rookie defensive tackle Gracen Halton, who emerged as one of the defensive bright spots of the 2026 rookie class, suffered a season-ending broken ankle late in the fourth quarter on Sunday.

The injury halted what was otherwise a celebration for the NFC-leading 49ers (7-1). With Las Vegas facing fourth-and-long inside the final minutes, Halton went down awkwardly on a rush attempt. The scene turned somber immediately and players from both sidelines took a knee, and the entire 49ers roster cleared the sideline to surround the cart and support the visibly emotional rookie as he was transported off the field.

Head coach Kyle Shanahan confirmed postgame that Halton sustained a fractured ankle, shutting down his rookie campaign just as he was carving out a crucial role in San Francisco's interior rotation.

A Sensation in the Making: Halton's Stellar Rookie Campaign

Selected in the fourth round (No. 107 overall) out of Oklahoma, Halton wasted no time proving his explosiveness translated to the pro level. In pre-draft testing, his athletic profile jumped off the charts, and defensive line coach Kris Kocurek quickly integrated him into high-leverage situations.

Through his first eight NFL games, starting six, Halton was actively making game-changing plays in both phases:

Before going down on Sunday, Halton was creating havoc once again. On the snap immediately following a Brock Purdy interception in the third quarter, Halton tipped and nearly intercepted a Kirk Cousins pass at the line of scrimmage, setting up Fred Warner's fumble-forcing punch one play later.

Earlier in the year, Halton cemented his place on highlight reels with a scoop-and-score fumble recovery touchdown, showcasing rare quickness and lateral agility for a 292-pound interior defender.

What It Means for the 49ers' Defensive Line

Losing Halton is a significant blow to the 49ers' interior defensive depth, but the front office's proactive aggression ahead of the NFL trade deadline softens the impact.

Just days before Halton's injury, general manager John Lynch shipped a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to reacquire veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. While the move originally looked like an opportunity to build a dominant, fresh rotation between Buckner, Halton, and Kevin Givens, Halton's injury now thrusts Buckner into an indispensable, every-down role inside alongside Nick Bosa.

Halton will undergo surgery and turn his focus toward rehabilitation with an eye on returning at full strength for the 2027 season. For San Francisco, the challenge will be matching the sheer disruption, motor, and edge that their rookie tackle brought to the field every Sunday.

text:
Lucas Patrick is out Thursday night against the New York Giants. The Commanders’ final injury report also ruled out tight end Colson Yankoff, leaving Washington to start Nick Allegretti at center in place of Patrick.

Patrick entered concussion protocol during Sunday’s loss to the Rams, and rookie Matt Gulbin finished that game at center. Head coach Dan Quinn confirmed Tuesday that Allegretti will start against New York. Gulbin got the call Sunday because he had been taking the center reps while Allegretti worked at guard, a decision I wrote more about earlier this week. According to Washington's official website, the Giants blitz at the third-highest rate in the NFL. Allegretti will have to help set the protection against that defense with Jayden Daniels behind him.

Treylon Burks missed Wednesday’s practice with the foot injury that kept him out against the Rams, but he has no game designation. Quinn said the day off was planned after Burks got work Tuesday and that the receiver was expected to be ready Thursday. Washington did not practice Monday and held a walkthrough Tuesday, so those first two participation reports were estimates. Burks’ place on the active list will be confirmed with Thursday’s inactives.

Yankoff did not practice during the short week because of a knee injury. His absence reaches beyond the tight end rotation: Washington credited him with 185 special teams snaps this season. John Bates (shoulder) was full all three days, and Chig Okonkwo (hip) was full Tuesday and Wednesday. Neither has a game designation.

Daniels (left elbow) and Gulbin (knee) practiced fully throughout the week. Shy Tuttle (shoulder) was full Tuesday and Wednesday, while Amik Robertson (ankle) also finished without a game designation.

New York listed linebacker Malik Harrison (groin) as questionable after he was limited all week. Quarterback J.J. McCarthy (hip) and running back Cam Skattebo (hamstring) finished without game designations, as did Abdul Carter (knee/back), who was listed as full Wednesday after two limited days.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The Green Bay Packers kicked off their biggest week of the season with their longest injury report of the year.

Officially, the Packers did not practice on Wednesday as they get ready for Sunday’s showdown against the Minnesota Vikings. If they would have, five starters would not have practiced and a total of 16 players were dealing with one issue or another.

Nickel Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), running back Josh Jacobs (finger), center Sean Rhyan (ankle), edge Lukas Van Ness (back) and tight end Josh Whyle (concussion) would not have practiced.

Rhyan was injured during the opening series at Detroit. So, he missed most of that game and then the next two games. Coach Matt LaFleur said Rhyan could “potentially” return this week, but that he would not have practiced on Wednesday might not be a good sign for Sunday.

That means John Williams could be in line for his third career start – and his first against the most aggressive defense in the league.

“Banked reps and experience, you can't beat that,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “If we were on a away game, it would be even more critical because sometimes John having his head between his legs, those are the guys that got to communicate a lot of looks. So, it'll be good for John to be at home, he'll be able to see everything and make all those calls.”

Franklin has missed the last three games due to an injury sustained at practice before the Detroit game.

Finally, Van Ness was a noteworthy addition. He played 32 of the 63 snaps against New England and contributed one tackle. He leads the team with 4.5 sacks.

More Starters Were Limited

The questions on the offensive line run deeper than center. Left guard Aaron Banks (knee/hip) would have been limited participation, a continuation of a season filled with injuries. He’s played only 137 snaps. Of his three starts, he was unable to go the distance against the Jets in Week 2 or the Patriots last week.

When Banks was knocked out of the New England game, Kevin Zeitler made his Packers debut. Well, he would have been limited participation, as well, with an ankle injury.

Linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper, who played only two defensive snaps vs. the Patriots due to a pregame chest injury, would have been limited due to illness; the chest is not mentioned on the injury report.

Kicker Trey Smack (right calf) and receiver Savion Williams (groin) were listed as limited participation, as well.

One starter not on the injury report is Love. He was knocked to the turf at one point last week and got up flexing his left hand.

“It was just one of those weird ones where it just get hits, so it’s fine,” he said.

Skyy Moore Designated for Return

Receiver Skyy Moore was designated for return after missing the last four games with an ankle injury. He is averaging 16.0 yards per punt return, highlighted by a 63-yarder against the Jets, and 27.5 yards per kickoff return. Both figures lead the team.

On offense, he caught seven passes for only 35 yards.

“He's been such a great returner for us,” Love said. “It'll definitely be huge to get him back and I'm grateful that we're able to get him back this week.”

Running back Chris Brooks (ankle) and edge Micah Parsons (knee/illness), who are entering their second week of practice after being designated for return, would have been limited. Brooks would be a big addition against the Vikings’ blitzing defense.

Vikings Injury Update

The big news in Minnesota – other than trading for Kirk Cousins – is that star linebacker Blake Cashman is in the concussion protocol. That’s never good news for any team or player, but that’s especially noteworthy considering the Vikings are coming off a Monday night game, so Cashman will have a day less to recover.

“He had the stinger evaluation going on and then did end up taking a hit, or more than likely giving a hit, later on in that game. He is currently in the concussion protocol,” Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell told reporters. “Obviously, short week. He's doing really, really well, but I'll keep you guys posted on him as we go through the week.”

Cashman leads the Vikings with 76 tackles, including seven tackles and two tackles for losses in Week 1. He’s in the top three on the team with 4.5 sacks, eight tackles for losses, 10 quarterback hits and seven passes defensed. Cashman is 10th in the league in tackles. From that group, nobody has more sacks, tackles for losses, quarterback hits or pass breakups.

In fact, no player with even 50 tackles has 10 quarterback hits. Cashman and Tampa Bay’s Josiah Trotter (70 tackles) are the only players with 60-plus tackles and seven PBUs. He is an elite player.

“Cash is an important part of our defense,” defensive coordinator Brian Flores said last season. “He’s a big part of what we do defensively from a communication standpoint, just an athleticism, football acumen. Getting other guys in the right positions, leadership. He does a great job.”

Packers Wednesday Injury Report

Did not participate: S Javon Bullard (ankle/knee), LB Zaire Franklin (shin), RB Josh Jacobs (finger), C Sean Rhyan (ankle), edge Lukas Van Ness (back), TE Josh Whyle (concussion).

Limited participation: LG Aaron Banks (knee/hip), RB Chris Brooks (ankle), G/T Travis Glover (knee), LB Ty’Ron Hopper (illness), WR Skyy Moore (ankle), edge Micah Parsons (knee/illness), K Trey Smack (right calf), WR Savion Williams (groin), G Kevin Zeitler (ankle).

Full participation: WR Bo Melton (gameday concussion evaluation).

Note: Brooks, Moore and Parsons have been designated to return and are within their 21-day practice window.

Vikings Wednesday Injury Report

Did not participate: LB Blake Cashman (concussion), TE T.J. Hockenson (wrist/chest), DL Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins (ankle), WR Jauan Jennings (calf), QB Kyler Murray (hamstring), OLB Kyle Van Noy (calf).

Limited participation: S Jay Ward (knee), QB Carson Wentz (ankle).

Full participation: S Theo Jackson (quad).
